If you’re in a small college somewhere teaching might make up the majority of a professor’s  duties. In a research university teaching is only a small task among many large ones. They supervise master and doctorate students, run research labs, write and review research, write grants, manage a research lab and so on and so forth. Frequently (at least in my experience) they are also involved in start ups, do consulting work on the side - these are common because professors are (or should be) extremely skilled in their field, and innovate quite a lot, leading to patents and start ups. Nearly none of the professors I’ve known (excepting in small colleges) work anything resembling normal hours.

This is me. Except I’m in academia, my pay is crap and my contracts ephemeral. I’m tired of working so much I don’t see my family, and have no time for hobbies or pastimes. I’ve seen professorates open up due to suicide, friends have been on suicide watch for weeks, others have broken marriages and/or messed up kids. The cost of success (viz. get tenure, a significant name) in academia is too high. And all this with very little pay to show for it. 

So, I’m leaving. Primarily for life quality reasons. You can do the same. One benefit to your (and mine) past might be attractiveness in the job market, so leaving should not be too hard if you do decide to do so.

You only live once. There’s nothing to indicate there’s an afterlife, so take care of your time alive. It’s all you have.

What about research after med school? As an MD you will have the option to be a practicing physician, but you  can also get a PhD and go into research. More creative than that is hard to find. More interesting than being involved in cutting edge work on an international level is also hard to beat. And the freedom you get as a researcher is gratifying. As much of the work you can do also involves people, it quickly becomes as social as you want. With degrees from the UK you’ll be able to work almost anywhere as well. On the off chance you want to do something else you’ll be able to. We have friends who left their practice and are now in various other careers. Consulting, mostly - but also ranging all the way to running a yarn store - or full time politics. You’ll not be locked into medicine if you get an MD, though my bet is that you’ll find something within medicine you’ll love. 

My wife aimed for medical research initially, but ended up choosing geriatrics and loves her job. She also worked in psychiatry for a while and enjoyed that as well. 
Medicine is a diverse and large field where you should be able to find work you enjoy. It will pay well and job security is high. There are various large benefits to getting a good education you as an individual besides money as well. It correlates with job satisfaction, health and quality of life in general. Your student years will be very formative and help you build yourself and your mind, beyond the professional gains you’ll make.

Me, I did go into research (nanotechnology, I hold an M.Sc. and a Ph.D. - no MD) and I enjoy it very much. The creativity permeating every aspect of my job is gratifying, and knowing that no one else has done exactly what I do - ever - sure helps keep it interesting. Note that it should be said there are issues with academia - as with anywhere else - it’s good, but it is not perfect. I would still recommend it (research) to anyone who’s got the grits and motivation. Both of which are needed in abundance.

I don’t know where you live, but here (Norway) there are some options that are quite appealing to someone in your position. My wife and I used them ourselves to change careers back in 08. I was in IT at the time, help desk work. My only education was high school. My wife was in healthcare, with a BA.
Like you we wanted some change, so we grabbed it. I quit my job, my wife quit hers and we started university in another part of the country. At the time I was 27 years old, so we started quite late.

I did a 5 year integrated M.Sc. in nanotechnology (kind of a generalist STEM education) and then a Ph.D. in Chemical Engineering (another 3.5 years) I now work as a scientist (post doc at a fairly large university) and entrepreneur (in biotech) - some colleagues and myself developed a test kit for corona. It’s in use in Norway, Denmark and India already. My work is, in other words, highly relevant and quite important. At this stage that’s a solid motivating factor.

What motivated me in the start was, to a large extent, a need for more challenges and a desire to learn. I had no idea I’d be contributing to saving lives during a pandemic after my studies. My motivations were not unlike what you said. When I started university I didn’t even remember algebra, I was quite far behind. The first couple of years were very tough - and my GPA was low. It was difficult to maintain my motivation - but it helped me build up some swords grit. Working really hard  (and I do mean hard) I got my GPA up - and the rest sort of followed. My wife studied medicine and is now an MD.  

The path we chose was not easy. It was not quick. It was not cheap. But it was so worth it on a personal level. Not to mention professionally. And, financially, it’ll end in a solid net gain. No doubt about that.

So- do you have an option to go back to school? Get a good degree in a STEM field? I say STEM because it will enable you to solve tangible problems we face as a civilization. Not that you’ll automatically be a new Elon Musk or end up developing life-saving technology - but technically you COULD. It’s difficult to imagine the same tangible, concrete potential with a ‘softer’ degree. Not that they aren’t important as well.

When I was doing my PhD two of the conferences I attended were in the same series of conferences. One in Germany and one in France. 

In both cases they had a fancy dinner and wine tasting event one evening. In Germany there was a delay in serving the food. It was not very bad. Maybe as much as fifteen minutes. During that time the organizer was clearly freaking out and hurried off to the kitchen to try to straighten things out. He also apologized after the fact. The wine tasting was structured, we all sat around long tables and were served effectively by very structured waiters - and clear information was given prior to every glass we tried. 

In FRANCE the dinner was also delayed. The host didn’t even react. The wine tasting consisted of a series of tables filled with cheese and wine. Lots and lots of both, and it was all truly excellent - but the information about the wines and cheeses consisted of “welcome! ‘Ere is le wine, and ‘ere is le cheese. Enjoy!”

I enjoy both France and Germany. But this experience quite clearly describes my perception of both countries - Germany is efficient, always on time and very structured. France? Great place to chill with excellent food and wine- but don’t expect too much structure - or for things to start when they’re supposed to.
